message.content:
### Choosing a Data Structure for Currency Valuations Over Time When you’re storing exchange‑rate data (or any financial time‑series), you want a structure that: | Requirement | What you need | Typical choice | |-------------|---------------|----------------| | **Fast look‑ups by date** | O(1) or O(log n) | `dict` (hash table) or `bisect` on sorted list | | **Ordered by time** | Preserve chronological order | `list`, `deque`, or `pandas.Series/DataFrame` | | **Efficient range queries** | Get all values between two dates | `sortedcontainers.SortedDict`, `pandas` with slicing | | **Easy aggregation** | Compute moving averages, returns, etc. | `pandas` (vectorised ops) | | **Scalable storage** | Persist millions of rows | Time‑series DB (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) or columnar store (Parquet) | | **Interoperability** | Export to CSV, JSON, SQL | `pandas` + `to_csv`, `to_json`, `to_sql` | Below are the most common options, with pros/cons and sample code. --- ## 1. In‑Memory Python Structures | Structure | Pros | Cons | Example | |-----------|------|------|---------| | **Dictionary of `datetime` → `float`** (`{date: rate}`) | • O(1) lookup
• Simple API | • No inherent ordering
• Range queries require sorting | ```python\nfrom datetime import datetime\nrates = {\n datetime(2024, 1, 1): 1.10,\n datetime(2024, 1, 2): 1.12,\n}\nprint(rates[datetime(2024, 1, 1)])\n``` | | **List of `(datetime, float)` tuples** (`[(date, rate), …]`) | • Ordered by insertion
• Easy to iterate | • O(n) lookup unless sorted + binary search | ```python\nimport bisect\nfrom datetime import datetime\nvals = [(datetime(2024, 1, 1), 1.10), (datetime(2024, 1, 2), 1.12)]\n# Binary search for a date\nidx = bisect.bisect_left([d for d, _ in vals], datetime(2024, 1, 2))\nprint(vals[idx][1])\n``` | | **`sortedcontainers.SortedDict`** | • Keeps keys sorted automatically
• O(log n) lookup & range queries | • Adds dependency | ```python\nfrom sortedcontainers import SortedDict\nfrom datetime import datetime\nsd = SortedDict({datetime(2024, 1, 1): 1.10, datetime(2024, 1, 2): 1.12})\nprint(sd[datetime(2024, 1, 1)])\n# Range query\nfor d, r in sd.items(datetime(2024, 1, 1), datetime(2024, 1, 2)):\n print(d, r)\n``` | **When to use** - Small datasets that fit comfortably in RAM. - Quick prototyping or scripts that don’t need heavy analytics. --- ## 2. Pandas – The “Swiss Army Knife” for Time Series | Feature | Why it matters | Code snippet | |---------|----------------|--------------| | **`Series` / `DataFrame` with `DatetimeIndex`** | Built‑in time‑indexing, resampling, rolling windows | ```python\nimport pandas as pd\nfrom datetime import datetime\nidx = pd.DatetimeIndex([datetime(2024, 1, 1), datetime(2024, 1, 2)])\nser = pd.Series([1.10, 1.12], index=idx)\nprint(ser.loc[datetime(2024, 1, 1)])\n``` | | **Vectorised operations** | Compute daily returns, moving averages in one line | ```python\nreturns = ser.pct_change()\nma_7 = ser.rolling(window=7).mean()\n``` | | **Resampling** | Convert daily to monthly, quarterly, etc. | ```python\nmonthly = ser.resample('M').last()\n``` | | **Missing‑data handling** | Forward/backward fill, interpolation | ```python\nser_ffill = ser.ffill()\n``` | | **Export helpers** | `to_csv`, `to_parquet`, `to_sql` | ```python\nser.to_csv('rates.csv')\n``` | **When to use** - Medium‑size datasets (tens of thousands to millions of rows). - Need for statistical analysis, visualisation, or machine learning pipelines. - Working in Jupyter notebooks or data‑science workflows. --- ## 3. Persistent Storage – Time‑Series Databases | DB | Strengths | Typical API | |----|-----------|-------------| | **TimescaleDB** (PostgreSQL extension) | • SQL interface
• Compression, continuous aggregates
• Good for long‑term retention | `INSERT INTO rates (time, rate) VALUES ($1, $2);` | | **InfluxDB** | • Native time‑series features
• Downsampling, retention policies | `write_api.write(bucket="rates", record="rate,time=2024-01-01T00:00:00Z value=1.10")` | | **ClickHouse** | • Columnar, high‑throughput inserts
• Aggregations at query time | `INSERT INTO rates (time, rate) VALUES ('2024-01-01', 1.10)` | | **Parquet + S3** | • Columnar storage, compression
• Works with Spark, Dask | `df.to_parquet('s3://bucket/rates.parquet')` | **When to use** - Production systems that ingest millions of rows per day. - Need for long‑term archival, fast roll‑up queries, or distributed processing. - Integration with BI tools (Tableau, PowerBI) or data lakes. --- ## 4. Hybrid Approach – In‑Memory + Persistent A common pattern: 1. **Ingest** new rates into a **pandas DataFrame** (fast, vectorised). 2. **Persist** to a **TimescaleDB** or **Parquet** file for durability. 3. **Cache** recent data in a **Redis** hash or **SQLite** for quick access. ```python # Example pipeline import pandas as pd import psycopg2 # 1. Load new data new_rates = pd.read_csv('new_rates.csv', parse_dates=['date']) new_rates.set_index('date', inplace=True) # 2. Append to TimescaleDB conn = psycopg2.connect("dbname=fx user=postgres") cur = conn.cursor() for ts, row in new_rates.iterrows(): cur.execute("INSERT INTO rates (time, rate) VALUES (%s, %s)", (ts, row['rate'])) conn.commit() # 3. Cache in Redis (optional) import redis r = redis.Redis() for ts, row in new_rates.iterrows(): r.hset('rates_cache', ts.isoformat(), row['rate']) ``` --- ## Quick Decision Guide | Size of dataset | Need for analytics? | Persistence required? | Recommended structure | |-----------------|---------------------|------------------------|-----------------------| | < 10 k rows | No | No | `dict` or `list` | | 10 k–1 M rows | Yes | Optional | `pandas.DataFrame` | | > 1 M rows | Yes | Yes | Time‑series DB (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB) + `pandas` for analysis | | Real‑time streaming | Yes | Yes | Kafka → InfluxDB → TimescaleDB | --- ## Bottom Line - **For quick scripts or small projects**: a simple `dict` or `list` of `(datetime, rate)` tuples works fine. - **For data‑science workflows**: use **pandas**; it gives you everything from indexing to rolling windows. - **For production, high‑volume, long‑term storage**: store in a **time‑series database** (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB) and pull into pandas only when you need to analyse or visualise. Pick the one that matches your data volume, performance needs, and persistence requirements. Happy coding!
